lead: Both readings are about wakefulness and about the work that cannot wait. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord comes without warning, and that those who belong to the light are to stay awake and sober. In Luke, Jesus rises before dawn to pray alone, and then refuses to stay where he is welcomed because he was sent to proclaim the kingdom to other towns as well. The key words are keep awake and I must proclaim.

r.h: Children of light and of the day
set: First Thessalonians was written by Paul from Corinth, probably around AD 50–51, and is one of the earliest writings of the New Testament. The young church at Thessalonica was anxious about believers who had died (4:13–18) and about when the Lord would return. Paul has comforted them about the first and now turns to the second.

He does not give a timetable. He says that they know very well that the day of the Lord will come “like a thief in the night”, and then tells them how to live in the meantime. Many scholars hear in “peace and security” (v. 3) an echo of the slogans of the Roman Empire; whether or not this is so, the words describe the false calm that comes before a sudden crisis.
str: vv. 1–2: no need to write about times and seasons: the day comes like a thief in the night.
v. 3: those who say “peace and security” will be taken by sudden destruction, like labour pains.
vv. 4–5: but you are not in darkness; you are children of light and of the day.
v. 6: so let us not sleep but keep awake and be sober.
kw: The image comes from Jesus’ own teaching (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). It is not the picture of a threat to believers but of a surprise for those who do not expect the Lord.
To be spiritually alert. In the Gospels Jesus repeats this call at Gethsemane and in his teaching on the end (Mark 13:35–37).
Literally not drunk. A clear mind, clear of the intoxication of the world’s false promises, is the mark of those who live in the light.
vv: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
No one knows the day. The right response is not to calculate but to live ready.
you are all children of light and children of the day
Paul reminds them who they are before telling them what to do. Their identity is given by God in Baptism, and their behaviour follows from it.
let us keep awake and be sober
Paul says “let us”, and includes himself. Wakefulness is a task for the whole Church, together.
ch: The Church has always taught that no one knows the time of the end. The Catechism says that we know neither the moment of the consummation of the earth and of humanity nor the way in which the universe will be transformed (CCC 1048). The right reaction to this is the one Paul asks of the Thessalonians: faith, hope and love (5:8), and prayer. The Church’s whole liturgical year is a school of watchfulness, and the call “watch” returns constantly, with the parable of the ten virgins in Matthew 25:13.

r.h: I must proclaim the good news
set: The passage closes Luke’s first day of ministry at Capernaum: Jesus has taught in the synagogue, driven out a demon and healed Simon’s mother-in-law and many others (4:31–41). The crowds are now at his door. In the morning he goes alone to a deserted place, as he does at other key moments in Luke (5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28).

The crowds find him and want to keep him. Jesus answers that his mission is larger than one town. A textual note: many manuscripts read “synagogues of Galilee” in verse 44 (as in Mark 1:39), but the NRSV text has “Judea”, and Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the land of the Jews as a whole.
str: v. 42: at daybreak Jesus goes to a deserted place; the crowds seek him and try to keep him.
v. 43: “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also”.
v. 44: he continues preaching in the synagogues.
kw: A place of prayer, silence and meeting with God, as in the story of Moses and Elijah. Jesus’ own source of strength is in this solitude.
A word Luke uses of God’s plan. Jesus does not follow popularity but the Father’s will.
Jesus knows that he is sent. The mission precedes the crowds’ desires.
vv: At daybreak he departed and went into a deserted place.
After a day of healing, Jesus goes to pray. His public work comes out of a hidden life with the Father.
the crowds were looking for him
The crowds are not wrong to want him; they are right to seek him. But they would keep him for themselves.
I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.
Jesus’ mission is for everyone. He cannot be kept in one place, however much he is loved there.
ch: The Catechism points to the prayer of Jesus before decisive moments in his ministry, as Luke’s Gospel stresses (CCC 2602), and to his proclamation of the kingdom as the centre of his mission (CCC 541–542). The Church sees in this passage the rhythm of her own life: prayer first, then mission. A parish that wishes to proclaim the Gospel to the other “cities” must also keep its deserted places of prayer. The sentence “I was sent” is repeated in the Church’s own sending: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

rite: In the West Syriac tradition the Church keeps vigil in the night hours of prayer, the Lilyo, as well as the morning hours of the Sapro. Paul’s words about being awake and sober are lived each time the faithful rise to pray while others sleep, and Jesus’ early morning prayer in the deserted place is the model of these hours.
study: Paul says that we are children of light and of the day. What is one way in which I can live as one who is awake this week, and not as one who sleeps?
Jesus withdrew to pray before going on to other towns. Where is my own “deserted place”, and what mission might come out of it?
